stem: Which of the following expressions is equivalent to `!(a > 5 || b <= 3)`?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This negates the comparisons incorrectly: the negation of `a > 5` is `a <= 5`, not `a < 5`, and the negation of `b <= 3` is `b > 3`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This changes `||` to `&&` but leaves the comparisons un-negated.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: De Morgan's law: `!(P || Q)` is `!P && !Q`. The negation of `a > 5` is `a <= 5` and the negation of `b <= 3` is `b > 3`.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This negates each comparison but keeps the `||`. De Morgan's law also changes `||` to `&&`.

explanation: Apply De Morgan's laws: negating a compound condition negates each part and swaps `&&` and `||`.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This counts only one increment. The first `x++` leaves `x` at 1, and the second statement's first `x++` makes it 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes the right operand of `&&` is always evaluated. Because `x++ > 0` is false (0 > 0), the `&&` skips its right operand, so `x` is incremented only once there.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: In the first statement, `x++ > 0` compares 0 > 0 (false) and leaves `x` at 1; the `&&` is short-circuited, so `r` is false. In the second, `x++ >= 0` compares 1 >= 0 (true) and leaves `x` at 2; the `||` is short-circuited, so `s` is true.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes both operands of both `&&` and `||` are always evaluated. Each operator skips its right operand when the left operand already decides the result.

explanation: `&&` skips its right operand when the left is false and `||` skips it when the left is true, so side effects in the right operand may never happen.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This assumes `b > 7` is true. Here `b` is 6, so the `else` branch runs when `a > 3`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This pairs the `else` with the outer `if (a > 3)`, as the indentation of some code might suggest. In Java an `else` always belongs to the nearest unmatched `if`.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This pairs each `else` with its outer `if`. An `else` belongs to the nearest `if`, which is `if (b > 7)` in both statements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The `else` belongs to the inner `if (b > 7)`. In the first statement `a > 3` is true and `b > 7` is false, so the `else` runs: c = 2. In the second, `a > 5` is false, so nothing in that statement runs and d stays 0.

explanation: An `else` is matched with the nearest preceding `if` that has no `else`; indentation does not matter.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This adds the number even when the `Buzz` branch ran. The `else` belongs to the second `if`, so `n` is appended only when `n % 5 != 0`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This treats the two tests as one `if`/`else if` chain. The second `if` is independent of the first, so both "Fizz" and "Buzz" can be added.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This pairs the `else` with the first `if`. In the code, the `else` follows the second `if`, so for 9 the `else` appends 9.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: For 15 both `if` statements add text ("FizzBuzz"); the `else` is skipped. For 10, only the second `if` is true: "Buzz". For 9, the first `if` adds "Fizz", and the second `if` is false, so its `else` appends 9: "Fizz9".

explanation: Consecutive `if` statements are independent; only the `else` that directly follows an `if` is tied to that `if`.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This overlooks `x > 20` in `b2`. All three parts must be true for the `&&` chain, and `7 > 20` is false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `&&` binds tighter than `||`. `b1` is `(7 > 5 && 7 < 10) || (...)`, which is true. `b2` requires `7 > 20`, so it is false. `b3` is `false || (7 < 10 && 7 != 7)`, which is false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This evaluates `||` before `&&` in `b1`. `&&` has higher precedence, so `b1` is `(x > 5 && x < 10) || (x == 12 && x > 20)`, which is true.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This overlooks `x != 7` in `b3`. The right side is `x < 10 && x != 7`, which is false for 7.

explanation: `!` is evaluated first, then `&&`, then `||`. Use parentheses to be sure of the grouping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: `equals` compares only names, so `a.equals(b)` is true. `a == b` is false (different objects). `a == c` is true (the same object). `a.equals(d)` is false (different names), and `a.equals("Ann")` is false because a `String` is not a `Person`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes the default `Object.equals`, which compares references. `Person` overrides `equals` to compare names, so `a.equals(b)` is true.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes `equals` compares both fields. The class's `equals` compares only the names, so two people with the same name are equal even when their ages differ.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: `==` always compares references and never calls `equals`, so `a == b` is false: they are two different objects.

explanation: `==` compares references, whatever `equals` does. An overridden `equals` defines what it means for two different objects to be equal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reads the condition as a comparison. A single `=` assigns, and the value of an assignment expression is the value assigned (`true`).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: `done = true` assigns true to `done` and evaluates to true, so the `if` branch prints A, and `done` is true afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The assignment `done = true` does change `done`, so the second statement prints `true`.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A condition must be a `boolean` expression, and `done = true` is one (an assignment of a `boolean` value has type `boolean`), so this compiles.

explanation: An assignment is an expression whose value is the assigned value. With `boolean`, `if (flag = true)` compiles but is almost always a bug.

stem: Which of the following is equivalent to `(a && b) || (!a && !b)`, where `a` and `b` are `boolean` variables?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is true when exactly one of them is true, the opposite.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is also true when only one is true, which the original expression rejects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The expression is true exactly when `a` and `b` are both true or both false, which is when they have the same value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is true only when both are true. The original is also true when both are false.

explanation: A truth table shows that the expression is true when `a` and `b` agree.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: For 70 through 79 the next `if` assigns "C", and values below 80 never satisfy `n >= 80`.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: For `n >= 90` the first branch assigns "A", so the `else if` is skipped.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: "B" is assigned when `n >= 80` and `n < 90` (the `else if` runs only when `n >= 90` is false). None of the later `if` statements reassigns `g` for those values.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: At `n = 90` the first condition `n >= 90` is true, so "A" is assigned and the `else if` is skipped.

explanation: Track the later `if` statements as well: separate `if` statements can overwrite earlier assignments, while an `else if` runs only when the previous condition was false.

choices.label: A
choices.text: The method compiles, but it throws an exception when `n` is 0.
choices.explanation: The compiler rejects the method; it never gets a chance to throw anything.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The method does not compile, because there is a path (when `n` is 0) that reaches the end without returning a value.
choices.explanation: The compiler requires every path through a non-`void` method to return a value. Here the case `n == 0` falls through both conditions, which is a compile-time error (missing return statement).

choices.label: C
choices.text: The method compiles and returns -1 for every value of `n` that is not positive.
choices.explanation: The `else if (n < 0)` only returns -1 for negative values, and 0 reaches no return statement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The method compiles and returns 0 when `n` is 0.
choices.explanation: A method does not return a default value; if no `return` runs, it is a compile-time error.

explanation: Every path through a method with a return type must end in a `return` (or a thrown exception).

stem: The variable `str` is a `String` that may be `null`. Which of the following conditions evaluates to `true` when `str` refers to a non-empty string, and to `false` (without throwing an exception) when `str` is `null`?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: When `str` is `null`, `str != null` is false and `&&` skips the right operand, so `str.length()` is never called. For a non-empty string both parts are true.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The left operand `str.length() > 0` is evaluated first and throws when `str` is `null`.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: When `str` is `null` the left operand is true, so `&&` evaluates `str.length()`, which throws. For a non-null string it is false even if the string is non-empty.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The `length()` call is evaluated first, so it throws a `NullPointerException` when `str` is `null`.

explanation: Put the `null` check first so that short-circuit evaluation protects the method call.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every `x` that is greater than 0 and also greater than 10
choices.explanation: The `else if` is evaluated only if `x > 0` is false, so it can never be reached by such a value.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: These values satisfy `x > 0`, so `r` is assigned 1 and the `else if` is skipped.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: These values also satisfy `x > 0`, so `r` is assigned 1; and `x > 10` is false for them anyway.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There is no such value of `x`.
choices.explanation: Any `x` greater than 10 is also greater than 0, so the first condition is true and the `else if` is never reached. The second condition can only be tested when `x <= 0`, and then `x > 10` is false.

explanation: An `else if` condition is evaluated only when every earlier condition was false. Here the order makes the second branch unreachable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This moves the negation to the whole condition. In the code the `!` applies only to `n % 5 == 0`, which is true for 12 (12 is not a multiple of 5).

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This treats `else if (n % 4 == 0)` as a separate `if`. Since `n % 3 == 0` is true, the `else if` is skipped and 4 is not added.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 12 is even: +1. 12 % 3 == 0: +2 (and the `else if` is skipped). 12 is divisible by 4 and 6: +8. 12 is not a multiple of 5: +16. The total is 27.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This treats `n % 4 == 0 && n % 6 == 0` as false. 12 is divisible by both 4 and 6, so 8 is added.

explanation: Independent `if` statements each add their own amount, while an `else if` is skipped when the previous condition is true.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: `equalsIgnoreCase` ignores case, so "Banana" and "BANANA" are equal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 'B' (66) is less than 'a' (97), so `"Banana".compareTo("apple")` is negative. `b.compareTo(c)` is 0 and `b == c` is true because the two literals are the same object. `equalsIgnoreCase` is true, and lowercase "banana" comes after "apple".

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes two string literals with the same characters are different objects. Identical literals refer to the same `String` object, so `b == c` is true.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This assumes alphabetical order ignoring case, so "Banana" would come after "apple". `compareTo` compares character codes, and uppercase letters have smaller codes than lowercase ones.

explanation: `compareTo` is case-sensitive and orders by character code; `equalsIgnoreCase` ignores case.

choices.explanation: This treats the first condition as `x >= 10`, so 10 returns "A" instead of falling through to the second test.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 11 > 10: "A". 10 is not greater than 10 but is >= 10: "B". 6 > 5: "C". 5 is not > 5, so it reaches the `else`: "D".

choices.explanation: This treats the third condition as `x >= 5`, so 5 returns "C". The code tests `x > 5`, so 5 reaches the `else`.

choices.explanation: This makes both boundary mistakes: 10 is treated as greater than 10, and 5 is treated as greater than 5.

explanation: Check each boundary value against `>` and `>=` carefully; the chain is evaluated top to bottom, and the first true condition wins.
